1H (Number Theory)

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 165
1H OurBigBook.com
Lagrange theorem for polynomial congruences says that a nonzero polynomial of degree d over the finite field Fp​ has at most d roots. To prove it, use mathematical induction on d. A constant nonzero polynomial has no roots. If f(a)=0, polynomial division in the field Fp​ gives f(X)=(X−a)q(X) with degq=d−1. Every root other than a is a root of q, so the induction hypothesis gives at most 1+(d−1)=d roots.
Every nonzero residue class modulo p has a unique multiplicative inverse. In the product (p−1)!, pair each class with its inverse. The unpaired classes satisfy x=x−1, hence x2−1=0. By the theorem these are exactly 1 and −1, and therefore
(p−1)!≡1⋅(−1)≡−1(modp).
(1)
This is Wilson theorem.
Now write p−1=kq. By Fermat's little theorem, every nonzero class is a root of
Xp−1−1=(Xk−1)(1+Xk+⋯+X(q−1)k).
(2)
The second factor has degree p−1−k and hence at most p−1−k roots. Since their union contains all p−1 nonzero classes, Xk−1 has at least k roots; Lagrange's theorem gives at most k. Thus xk≡1(modp) has exactly k solutions.

2H (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 147 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 147
2H OurBigBook.com
A subset A of a metric space is nowhere dense when the interior of its closure is empty. One form of the Baire category theorem says that a nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets; equivalently, a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.
Fix ε>0 and work in the complete interval [1,2]. For N≥1 define the closed set
EN​={x∈[1,2]:∣f(nx)∣≤ε for every n≥N}.
(3)
The sets are closed by the continuity of f, and the assumed pointwise convergence gives [1,2]=⋃N​EN​. The Baire category theorem therefore gives an N and a nonempty open interval (a,b)⊆[1,2] contained in EN​.
The intervals [na,nb] overlap once (n+1)a≤nb, which holds for every sufficiently large natural number n. Their union consequently contains a half-line. Every sufficiently large t can therefore be written as t=nx with n≥N and x∈(a,b), and then ∣f(t)∣=∣f(nx)∣≤ε. Since ε was arbitrary, f(t)→0 as t→∞.

Solution

Words: 126
a OurBigBook.com
A cipher has perfect secrecy when the conditional probability of every plaintext given a ciphertext equals its prior probability: Pr(M=m∣C=c)=Pr(M=m) whenever Pr(C=c)>0. Equivalently, the plaintext and ciphertext are independent random variables.
Fix a ciphertext c that can occur. Perfect secrecy requires every possible plaintext m to remain possible after observing c. For a deterministic decryption rule, two different plaintexts producing c require two different keys, so the key space has cardinality at least that of the message space.
In a one-time pad, the message and key belong to the same finite additive group, the key is uniform and independent of the message, and encryption is C=M+K. For every m,c there is exactly one key k=c−m, so
Pr(C=c∣M=m)=Pr(K=c−m)=∣K∣1​,
(4)
independent of m. Bayes' theorem then gives Pr(M=m∣C=c)=Pr(M=m), proving perfect secrecy.

b

Words: 118 Articles: 1
3I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 118
b OurBigBook.com
Perform every addition in the finite field F2​. From the two transmitted strings ci​=ai​+ki​ and di​=ai​+ki+1​ one obtains
ci​+di​=ki​+ki+1​(1≤i≤N).
(5)
Choosing one candidate value of k1​ recursively determines k2​,…,kN+1​, and hence determines the candidate plaintext ai​=ci​+ki​. There are only two candidates: changing k1​ complements every recovered key bit and every plaintext bit. The information that the message makes sense normally selects the intended candidate.
Once this ambiguity is resolved, any other ciphertext positions encrypted with the recovered segment k1​,…,kN+1​ can be decrypted. Key bits outside that segment remain independent and uniformly distributed, so this mistake gives no information about messages using only those bits. This is the two-time pad attack: reusing related one-time-pad key material destroys perfect secrecy.

4F (Automata and Formal Languages)

Words: 274 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 274
4F OurBigBook.com
A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form when every production has the form A→BC or A→a, where A,B,C are nonterminals and a is a terminal symbol; one may additionally allow the new start production S0​→ϵ when the language contains the empty string, provided S0​ never appears on a right-hand side.
The standard conversion proceeds as follows.
  • Introduce a fresh start symbol S0​ and S0​→S. This changes N only when the old start symbol occurs on a right-hand side or when a protected start symbol is needed to preserve ϵ.
  • Find all nullable nonterminals, add productions obtained by omitting nullable occurrences, and remove the original ϵ-productions except the permitted S0​→ϵ. This leaves N unchanged.
  • Eliminate each unit production A→B by adding to A the non-unit productions reachable through its transitive closure. This leaves N unchanged.
  • Delete non-generating symbols and then unreachable symbols. This is the only simplification stage that can shrink N.
  • In every right-hand side of length at least two, replace a terminal a by a fresh nonterminal Ta​ with Ta​→a. New nonterminals are needed exactly for terminals that occur in such mixed or long productions.
  • Break every right-hand side of length at least three into binary productions, introducing fresh nonterminals for successive suffixes. New nonterminals are needed exactly when such long productions remain.
The terminal alphabet Σ may be kept unchanged throughout, although unused terminals may be discarded by convention. Every stage preserves the generated language, with the explicit protection of ϵ at the start-symbol stage. For example,
S→SS∣a
(6)
is already in Chomsky normal form and generates the infinite language {an:n≥1}, so its conversion may be the grammar itself.

The individual t-tests only test each regression coefficient after adjusting for the other covariate. Here neither covariate is individually significant at conventional levels, but from the abbreviated coefficient table alone one cannot conclude that neither explains the response: strong multicollinearity can make both standard errors large even when the covariates are jointly useful.

ii

Words: 62 Articles: 1

ii OurBigBook.com
The full F-test has p<2.2×10−16 and tests the null hypothesis that both slope coefficients vanish. It decisively rejects that hypothesis, while R2=0.8126 says the fitted model explains about 81% of the sample variation. Together with the insignificant individual t-tests, this is characteristic of multicollinearity: the two covariates explain the response jointly, but the output does not identify either one as having a separately estimable effect.

Chemical equilibrium for p+e−⇌H+γ gives μp​+μe​=μH​, because the photon chemical potential vanishes. Applying the nonrelativistic number-density formula to all three massive species and taking the ratio gives
np​ne​nH​​=gp​ge​gH​​(kB​T2πℏ2​)3/2(mp​me​mH​​)3/2exp(kB​Tmp​c2+me​c2−mH​c2​).
(20)
Use charge neutrality np​=ne​, the Hydrogen binding energy Ebind​=mp​c2+me​c2−mH​c2, mH​≃mp​, and the ground-state statistical weights gH​=gp​ge​. Then
nH​≃ne2​(me​kB​T2πℏ2​)3/2eEbind​/kB​T​.
(21)
The approximations are a dilute, nondegenerate ideal gas in thermal and chemical equilibrium, nonrelativistic electrons, protons and hydrogen, negligible excited hydrogen states, and negligible corrections from the proton-to-hydrogen mass ratio. This relation is the Saha ionization equation.

An arithmetic function f is multiplicative when f(1)=1 and f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever m and n are coprime. If m and n are coprime, every divisor d of mn has a unique factorization d=d1​d2​ with d1​∣m and d2​∣n. Hence the Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative functions satisfies
(f⋆g)(mn)​=d1​∣m∑​d2​∣n∑​f(d1​d2​)g(d1​m​d2​n​)=(f⋆g)(m)(f⋆g)(n),​
(28)
and (f⋆g)(1)=1, so it is multiplicative.
Let ε be the identity for Dirichlet convolution, with ε(1)=1 and ε(n)=0 for n>1. The Möbius function satisfies μ⋆1=ε. Therefore, using commutativity and associativity,
f=μ⋆g⟹f⋆1=g⋆(μ⋆1)=g⋆ε=g.
(29)
This is the Möbius inversion formula.

ζ(s)2​=a,b≥1∑​(ab)s1​=n≥1∑​ns1​a∣n∑​1=n≥1∑​nsτ(n)​.​

Equivalently, Dirichlet convolution becomes multiplication of absolutely convergent Dirichlet series.

Zorn lemma states that if every chain in a nonempty partially ordered set has an upper bound in that set, then the set has a maximal element. It is equivalent, over the usual axioms of set theory, to the axiom of choice.

b

Words: 81 Articles: 1
16H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 81
b OurBigBook.com
The set Px​={y∈P:x≤y} is nonempty because it contains x. Every nonempty chain C⊆Px​ has an upper bound u in P by hypothesis. Since every member of C is at least x, one has x≤u, so u∈Px​. Zorn lemma therefore gives a maximal element σ of Px​. If σ≤z in P, then z∈Px​, and maximality in Px​ forces z=σ. Thus σ is maximal in P and satisfies x≤σ.

The family Un​={A⊆N:n∈A} is nonempty, excludes the empty set, is closed under finite intersections, and is upward closed. It is therefore a filter. For every A⊆N, either n∈A or n∈Ac, so either A∈Un​ or Ac∈Un​. Hence Un​ is the principal ultrafilter at n.

ii

Words: 82 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 82
ii OurBigBook.com
The cofinite filter F is nonempty, because N∈F; finite unions of finite complements show closure under intersections, and taking a superset can only shrink the complement. The empty set is excluded because its complement is infinite. It is not an ultrafilter: the even numbers and the odd numbers both have infinite complements, so neither belongs to F. Finally, N∖{n} is cofinite but does not belong to Un​, proving F⊈Un​ for every n.

iii

Words: 116 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 116
iii OurBigBook.com
Yes. Order the proper filters containing the cofinite filter by inclusion. The union of every chain is again a proper filter containing F: any finite collection of its members already lies in one filter in the chain. Zorn lemma gives a maximal proper filter U.
A maximal proper filter is an ultrafilter. Indeed, if A∈/U, adjoining A cannot generate another proper filter, so some U∈U has U∩A=∅. Thus U⊆Ac, and upward closure gives Ac∈U. Finally, U cannot equal any principal ultrafilter Un​, because it contains the cofinite set N∖{n} whereas Un​ does not. Thus U is a nonprincipal ultrafilter on N.

Words: 403 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 403
17G OurBigBook.com
Vizing theorem states that every finite simple graph of maximum degree Δ has
Δ≤χ′(G)≤Δ+1,
(73)
where χ′(G) is its edge chromatic number. The lower bound follows because all edges incident with a vertex of degree Δ need different colours.
For the upper bound, induct on the number of edges. Delete an edge xy and colour the remaining graph with the palette {1,…,Δ+1}. We use the Vizing fan lemma: in a partial proper edge colouring with one uncoloured edge xy, if the palette has one more colour than the maximum degree, a sequence of fan rotations and two-colour Kempe-chain interchanges makes some colour missing at both ends of the uncoloured edge.
Here is the fan argument. Build a maximal sequence y0​=y,y1​,…,yk​ of distinct neighbours of x such that, for i≥1, the colour on xyi​ is missing at an earlier fan vertex. Rotating an initial fan segment means moving each colour on xyi​ to the preceding edge where it is missing; this preserves properness and moves the uncoloured edge to the end of that segment. Choose a colour α missing at x and a colour β missing at yk​. On the maximal α-β alternating path from yk​, interchange α and β. If the path does not reach x, α is then missing at both x and yk​, so rotate the fan and colour its final uncoloured edge α. If it reaches x, its last edge at x has colour β. Maximality of the fan forces the other endpoint of that edge to be a fan vertex; rotate up to that vertex first. This breaks the alternating path before x, reducing to the preceding case. This proves the fan lemma and extends the colouring to xy, completing the induction.
For Kn,n​, label both vertex classes by Z/nZ and colour edge (i,j) by i+j. Each colour is a perfect matching, so this is an n-edge-colouring. Since Δ(Kn,n​)=n, χ′(Kn,n​)=n. If r=max{m,n}, embed Km,n​ into Kr,r​ and restrict its r-edge-colouring. The degree lower bound then gives
χ′(Km,n​)=max{m,n}​.
(74)
Finally, subdividing one edge of Kn,n​ produces n2+1 edges on 2n+1 vertices while keeping maximum degree n. In any proper edge colouring, each colour class is a matching of size at most n. An n-edge-colouring could therefore colour at most n2 edges, a contradiction. Thus χ′(G)>n, while Vizing theorem gives χ′(G)≤n+1, so
χ′(G)=Δ(G)+1=n+1​.
(75)

Thus B is contractible, A∩B is homotopy equivalent to the circle, and A is homotopy equivalent to the wedge sum of 2g circles. The boundary circle represents the product of the g commutators in the fundamental group of A, so its image in the first homology group, which is the abelianization of that group, is zero.

A family S⊆C(K) is equicontinuous if for every x∈K and ε>0 there is a neighborhood U of x such that
∣f(y)−f(x)∣<ε
(106)
for every y∈U and every f∈S. The Arzelà-Ascoli theorem says that, for a compact Hausdorff space K, a subset of C(K) has compact closure in the uniform norm if and only if it is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded. On compact K, equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness together imply uniform boundedness.
For necessity, a compact closure is totally bounded. Given ε>0, choose a finite ε/3-net f1​,…,fm​. The finitely many continuous functions fj​ are simultaneously continuous near each point, and comparison with a nearby fj​ proves equicontinuity of the whole family. Evaluation at any fixed point is a continuous map C(K)→R or C, so compactness also gives pointwise boundedness.
Conversely, equicontinuity gives, around each x∈K, a neighborhood on which every f∈S oscillates by less than ε/3. Compactness supplies a finite such cover with selected points x1​,…,xm​. Pointwise boundedness makes the set of vectors
{(f(x1​),…,f(xm​)):f∈S}
(107)
a bounded subset of a finite-dimensional normed vector space, so it has a finite ε/3-net. Choose one function of S for every nonempty cell of this net. If two functions have evaluation vectors in the same cell, then comparison at a selected xj​ and the two oscillation bounds show that their uniform distance is less than ε. Thus S is totally bounded. Since C(K) is a Banach space, its closure is complete; a complete totally bounded metric space is compact, proving the theorem.

Write C(K)=⋃n≥1​Sn​ with every Sn​ equicontinuous. Its closure En​=Sn​​ is still equicontinuous, because uniform limits preserve the same oscillation inequalities. The Baire category theorem applied to the Banach space C(K) shows that some En​ has nonempty interior. Hence there are f0​∈C(K) and r>0 such that the open ball B(f0​,r) lies in En​.
Fix x∈K. Equicontinuity of En​ gives a neighborhood U of x on which every member of En​ changes by less than r/4. If y∈U were distinct from x, the normality of a compact Hausdorff space and the Urysohn lemma would give h∈C(K) with h(x)=0, h(y)=r/2, and ∥h∥∞​=r/2. Both f0​ and f0​+h belong to En​, yet
∣h(y)−h(x)∣≤∣(f0​+h)(y)−(f0​+h)(x)∣+∣f0​(y)−f0​(x)∣<r/2,
(108)
a contradiction. Thus U={x}, so every point is isolated and K is a discrete space. A compact discrete space is finite, since its cover by singleton open sets has a finite subcover.

That is impossible for a compact regular surface in R3. Choose p∈S maximizing the Euclidean distance from the origin, after translating the origin off the surface if necessary. The sphere centered at the origin through p is a supporting sphere. The supporting-sphere curvature bound shows that both principal curvatures at p have the same sign and nonzero magnitude, so K(p)>0. Therefore g=1, and g=0. The classification theorem for surfaces now shows that S is diffeomorphic to the sphere.

An M/M/1 queue has Poisson process arrivals of rate λ, independent exponential service times of rate μ, and one server. The two letters M indicate the memoryless property of the interarrival and service-time distributions. Its queue length is a birth-death process with birth rate λ and death rate μ away from zero. When ρ=λ/μ<1, its normalized stationary distribution is
πn​=(1−ρ)ρn;
(152)
the powers ρn quoted in the question form the corresponding unnormalized invariant measure.

ii

Words: 115 Articles: 1
27K OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 115
ii OurBigBook.com
Let N be the number of visits to the server made by one customer. Then N has the geometric distribution with success parameter δ, and its service periods E1​,E2​,… are independent exponential random variables of rate μ. For s≥0, the Laplace transform of the total service time T=E1​+⋯+EN​ is
Ee−sT=∑k≥1​δ(1−δ)k−1(μ+sμ​)k=s+δμδμ​.
(153)
Thus
T∼Exp(δμ)​.
(154)
At each service completion, a successful departure reduces the queue length by one and occurs at rate δμ while the queue is nonempty; feedback completions leave its length unchanged. The queue-length process is therefore the birth-death process of an ordinary M/M/1 queue with service rate δμ. It is positive recurrent exactly when λ<δμ, and then, with ρ=λ/(δμ),
πn​=(1−ρ)ρn,n≥0​.
(155)

iii

Words: 116 Articles: 1
27K OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 116
iii OurBigBook.com
The Poisson output theorem for a feedback queue, equivalently the Burke theorem applied to the effective queue-length process with service rate δμ, shows that successful departures in equilibrium form a Poisson process of rate λ.
The process of all entries into the queue is different. Its long-run rate is
λ+(1−δ)μP(Q>0)=λ+(1−δ)μδμλ​=δλ​.
(156)
Immediately after any queue-entry event the server is busy, so the conditional probability of another entry in the next interval of length h is
[λ+(1−δ)μ]h+o(h):
(157)
the next entry can be external or can be a service completion followed by feedback. A Poisson process of the displayed long-run rate would instead give (λ/δ)h+o(h). These coefficients are unequal when λ<δμ, since
λ+(1−δ)μ−δλ​=(1−δ)(μ−δλ​)>0.
(158)
Hence the combined arrival process is not Poissonian.

Every density operator can be written as
ρ=∑j​pj​∣ψj​⟩⟨ψj​∣,pj​≥0,∑j​pj​=1.

Therefore ⟨ϕ∣ρ∣ϕ⟩=∑j​pj​∣⟨ψj​∣ϕ⟩∣2≥0, so ρ is a positive semidefinite operator, and Trρ=∑j​pj​=1. A pure quantum state has a rank-one density operator ∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣, equivalently ρ2=ρ and Tr(ρ2)=1. A mixed quantum state is not pure and has Tr(ρ2)<1 in finite dimension.
The Von Neumann equation and the Pauli matrix commutator identity give
ρ˙​=−ℏi​[H,ρ],[ω⋅σ,a⋅σ]=2i(ω×a)⋅σ,
(210)
so the Bloch vector obeys
a˙=2ω×a.
(211)
Writing ω=∣ω∣ and ω=ω/ω, the assumption a⋅ω=0 gives
a(t)=acos(2ωt)+(ω×a)sin(2ωt),
(212)
and hence
ρ(t)=21​[1H​+(acos(2ωt)+(ω×a)sin(2ωt))⋅σ]​.
(213)
Unitary evolution rotates the Bloch vector and preserves its length. Since ∣a∣<1, the state remains mixed, whereas ∣↑x​⟩ has the unit Bloch vector (1,0,0). The system is therefore never definitely in ∣↑x​⟩.

σ(k)=Imω=1+tanh(∣k∣h)∣k∣Utanh(∣k∣h)​​​,cp​=kReω​=1+tanh(∣k∣h)U​​.

σ∼2∣k∣U​,cp​∼2U​.

Thus the growth-rate curve starts at the origin with zero slope, rises like ∣k∣3/2, and approaches the straight-line asymptote ∣k∣U/2. The inviscid zero-thickness model consequently has no short-wave cutoff.

If the lower density ρ−​ exceeds the upper density ρ+​, stable density stratification adds a gravitational restoring term. Including surface tension γ, the same calculation has the schematic dispersion relation
ρ−​coth(Kh)(ω−kU)2+ρ+​ω2=(ρ−​−ρ+​)gK+γK3.
(275)
The gravity term dominates the shear term as K→0 and therefore suppresses sufficiently long waves. The capillary term dominates as K→∞ and suppresses sufficiently short waves. Together they reduce the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability growth rate and can leave only a finite unstable band, or eliminate instability if the restoring effects are strong enough.

The one-dimensional Isentropic Euler equations are
ρt​+uρx​+ρux​=0,ut​+uux​+ρc2​ρx​=0,c2=dρdp​.
(276)
Define the Riemann invariants for one-dimensional isentropic flow
R±​=u±∫ρ0​ρ​sc(s)​ds​.
(277)
Combining the two equations directly gives
[∂t​+(u±c)∂x​]R±​=0​,
(278)
so R±​ is constant on the corresponding characteristic curve dx/dt=u±c.
Initially both invariant disturbances are supported in 0≤x≤L. Once the two characteristic families have separated, the left-moving packet is a simple wave with R+​ at its equilibrium value, while the right-moving packet is a simple wave with R−​ at equilibrium. Between and outside them, both invariants retain their equilibrium values. The schematic spacetime diagram below uses the equilibrium slopes ±c0​ and shows separation after t=L/(2c0​).

Termwise differentiation of a Fourier series multiplies a mode by its wavenumber, so
(fx​)​m,n​=iπmf​m,n​,(fy​)​m,n​=iπnf​m,n​​.
(289)
The convolution theorem turns pointwise multiplication into discrete convolution:
h=fg=∑p,q​∑r,s​f​p,q​g​r,s​eiπ(p+r)x+iπ(q+s)y,

hm,n​=p,q∈Z∑​f​p,q​g​m−p,n−q​​.

The assumed real analyticity justifies these termwise operations through rapid decay of the Fourier coefficients.

Expand a,u,f in the two-dimensional Fourier basis. Applying the derivative and product rules from part (a), the (m,n) coefficient of the equation is
−π2∑p,q∈Z​(mp+nq)am−p,n−q​up,q​=f​m,n​.
(292)
The normalization and compatibility conditions are
u0,0​=0,f​0,0​=0​.
(293)
Thus, on Z2∖{(0,0)}, the infinite Fourier spectral method system is
p,q∑​A(m,n),(p,q)​up,q​=−f​m,n​​,A(m,n),(p,q)​=π2(mp+nq)am−p,n−q​​.
(294)
For a square spectral truncation, choose
ΛN​={(m,n):∣m∣,∣n∣≤N}∖{(0,0)},
(295)
retain equations and unknowns indexed by ΛN​, and set omitted coefficients to zero. This is the Fourier–Galerkin method: it projects the residual onto the retained Fourier modes. Other finite mode sets may be used in the same way.

Here the only nonzero coefficients of a are

Therefore, for each (m,n)∈ΛN​, the truncated system is
π2{​5(m2+n2)um,n​+[m(m−1)+n2]um−1,n​+[m(m+1)+n2]um+1,n​+[m2+n(n−1)]um,n−1​+[m2+n(n+1)]um,n+1​}=−f​m,n​,​

For wavevectors k=(m,n) and ℓ=(p,q), the matrix entry is
Ak,ℓ​=π2(k⋅ℓ)ak−ℓ​.

Because ar​=a−r​, Ak,ℓ​=Aℓ,k​, so the matrix is symmetric. Its diagonal entry is 5π2∣k∣2. The sum of absolute off-diagonal entries is at most
π2∑j=12​(∣k∣2+kj​+∣k∣2−kj​)=4π2∣k∣2,
(299)
because ∣k∣2±kj​≥0 for nonzero integer k; truncation can only reduce the sum. Hence A is strictly diagonally dominant with positive diagonal. The Gershgorin circle theorem places every eigenvalue in the positive interval
[π2∣k∣2,9π2∣k∣2]
(300)
for at least one row. Since the symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues, all are positive, and A is a positive-definite matrix. Any one-dimensional ordering merely conjugates A by a permutation matrix, preserving symmetry and positive definiteness.
